content:
Is a newborn child a sinner? The Reformed confessions answer that Adam's "corrupted nature" is conveyed to all his posterity, so that a child enters the world already marked by the fall.[1]

The question deserves a precise answer, because the churches do not give one answer to it, and Islam gives its own. A child's condition at birth, his guilt, and the age at which he answers for his acts are three separate questions.

This article aims to provide context to that question, insha'Allah, in five answers. Our article on original sin sets out the doctrine's history; here we ask only about the child. The Quran's frame is the one it gives for every soul: "On no soul doth Allah Place a burden greater than it can bear" (2:286).[2]

The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) said that every child is born upon the fiṭra, and that his parents then make him a Jew, a Christian or a Magian.[3] Abu Hurayra, who narrated the report, recited after it: "Allah's handiwork according to the pattern on which He has made mankind: no change (let there be) in the work (wrought) by Allah" (30:30).[2]

The fiṭra is the disposition God gave mankind, turned toward knowing and worshipping Him. It gives a child no learned theology, and it does not keep him from sin later in life. It means he begins with no debt from Adam, whose sin the Quran says was repented and forgiven (2:37).[2]

The law follows the same line. The Prophet said that the pen is lifted from three: the sleeper until he wakes, the child until he reaches puberty, and the insane until he comes to reason.[4] A child's deeds are not yet written against him.

The Catechism of the Catholic Church says that children are "born with a fallen human nature and tainted by original sin", and so "have need of the new birth in Baptism".[5]

It also says that original sin in Adam's descendants "does not have the character of a personal fault".[6] The Catholic newborn has committed nothing; he is born into a state of deprivation that the Church calls sin. A Muslim who says that Catholics hold infants personally guilty of Adam's act misstates the Catechism.

Orthodox Christians speak of "ancestral sin". Fr Steven Kostoff of the Orthodox Church in America writes that a child "is not born a 'guilty sinner'", and is born bearing the consequences of Adam's sin: corruption and death.[7]

The Orthodox funeral for an infant says so in its hymns. It states that "infants have done no evil", and calls the departed child "undefiled" and even "holy". Kostoff concludes: "There is no sin for which he needs to be forgiven."[7]

On the child's guilt, that position stands close to the Islamic one. The difference lies in what the child inherits, which for Orthodoxy is a mortal and wounded nature that needs Christ.

The Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod baptises infants, because baptism is God's act "not by any action or merit on the part of the Christian, which is why Baptism is conferred on babies, children and adults alike".[8]

The Southern Baptist confession, the Baptist Faith and Message (2000), takes another course. It says Adam's "posterity inherit a nature and an environment inclined toward sin", and that "as soon as they are capable of moral action, they become transgressors and are under condemnation". It defines baptism as "the immersion of a believer".[9]

Baptist pastors often call that threshold the "age of accountability". The phrase is pastoral, and the Bible has no such term. It still comes close to the Islamic rule of the lifted pen, where accountability begins with moral capacity.

The question is a tender one, and a poor weapon in debate. The Catholic Church says that "as regards children who have died without Baptism, the Church can only entrust them to the mercy of God", and that it may "hope that there is a way of salvation" for them.[10] The Orthodox service, as above, calls such a child undefiled.

The Prophet described a dream in which he saw Abraham in a garden surrounded by children, and was told that they were the children who die upon the fiṭra. When his Companions asked about the children of the idolaters, he said: "And also the children of pagans."[11] Muslim scholars held more than one view on the children of unbelievers, and this report is among the texts they weighed.

The Quran ties punishment to a warning received: God does not punish until He has sent a messenger (17:15).[2] A child who never reached the age of understanding has received no warning he could answer.

The bottom line

The answer depends on what "sinful" means. Islam holds that every child begins upon the fiṭra, carries no guilt from Adam, and answers for nothing until the pen is set to him. Catholicism teaches an inherited state it calls original sin and denies that it is the child's personal fault. Orthodoxy denies the child's guilt and affirms his inherited mortality. Protestants divide between infant baptism and an age of accountability.

On the child's guilt, much of Christianity has come near the Quran's rule: "No bearer of burdens can bear the burden of another" (17:15), and "The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father" (Ezekiel 18:20).[12] The difference that remains is whether a child needs a saviour at all. Islam says he needs none. Allahu alam.

Notes

  1. Westminster Confession of Faith (1646), chapter 6, section 3.
  2. Quran 2:286; 30:30; 2:37; 17:15, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
  3. Sahih al-Bukhari 1359 and 4775 (numbering of sunnah.com); Sahih Muslim 2658.
  4. Sunan Abi Dawud 4403, from Ali ibn Abi Talib; also in al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah.
  5. Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1250.
  6. Catechism of the Catholic Church, 405.
  7. Steven Kostoff, "An Infant's Burial", Orthodox Church in America, Reflections, 2 February 2009.
  8. Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod, "LCMS Views: Frequently Asked Questions", "What is Baptism, and what does it do?", lcms.org.
  9. The Baptist Faith and Message (Southern Baptist Convention, 2000), articles III and VII.
  10. Catechism of the Catholic Church, 1261.
  11. Sahih al-Bukhari 7047 and 1386, from Samura ibn Jundub (numbering of sunnah.com).
  12. Ezekiel 18:20 (World English Bible); Quran 17:15, translated by A. Yusuf Ali.
